Name: A Prophet
Review:
Breath-taking masterpiece. Prison & crime genre. Begins with a naieve and possibly innocent teenage boy thrust into an incomprehensibly harsh system. Forced to do the most horrific things, he learns everything he doesn't want to be and everything he doesn't want out of life from firsthand experience. Eventually, he carves out his own kind of morality and humanity from the despicable framework he is given. He doesn't become a hero, but he becomes as good - in both efficacy and ethics - as he can conceive given the environment he is damned to.

Beautifully shot. Haunting scenes. Graphic violence. Essentially a meditation on how to participate and survive in an evil world when the only truly moral choice is to surrender and die.

It's also a cool Superman film with great action scenes and visuals. It subverts several expectations we have about the characters and writes him with more depth than usually expected.

Name: Joker
Review:
People don't like this movie because they don't like the heteronormative white male rage it accurately depicts and the power fantasy that Fleck cum Joker represents. Snyder himself massively overcorrected by making Fleck the victim of every kind of emasculating crime imaginable in the sequel and having him repent for his crimes.

This movie essentially accurately depicts a kind of radicalization. Fleck was radicalized to burn society down because he was left out of it, essentially. He does not start the movie as a nihilist. He starts out as an average person, self centered but not malicious. Due to his generally good hearted nature and lack of opportunities, life showed him that actually the people who were more successful than him were crueler.

Arthur found out that there are no real world brownie points for goodness or hard work. He was left with the choice to either accept his caste in life or totally reject the system, and he chose to reject it.

Much of this same ethos underpinned the alt-right movement.

Review:

The third act was good although I think didn't live up to the promise of the premise. Amy Madigan did such an incredible job and I only wish we had more of her.

While I can appreciate David Lynch and the Lynchian direction, it isn't my favorite style. The director here mentioned that he's massively influenced by Lynch and we see that with some of the unintentional or random choices. I think what made David Lynch great is that, as random as some of his decisions were, there was usually some kind of a justification for it (although not always).

I'm excited to see what this director does next.

Name: One Battle After Another
Review:
What happens after you retire from your radical politics but the radical politics has not retired from you? A story that perhaps Paul Thomas Anderson was not qualified to tell but handled with as much grace as can be expected from a civilian. Critical of radical leftist politics while still giving us a socialist antihero in DiCaprio.

Imagine if the 2022 "How to Blow Up A Pipeline" had deeper characters, double the run time, world class acting, a healthy dose of black comedy, and less political commentary. I.e. an actually fun movie instead of a leftist fever dream. That's this movie.

The movie doesn't have much to say moral wise. It's a character drama, and comedy, between a father and his daughter primarily. There is no great lesson and this movie will not move you. But it taps into the ethos of our time.

As the star of right wing fascism is ascendant, where is the counterbalance of radical leftism as depicted here? Can such fervor be whipped up? Is it a good idea at all? Only time can tell.

The movie brings up these questions but doesn't purport to deal with them. It is focused on you having a raucous good time. That you will have.

Perhaps it could have been 15 minutes shorter.

Otherwise a remarkable movie.

Edit: the WH was not a fan. https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/09/countering-domestic-terrorism-and-organized-political-violence/

Name: Perfect Blue
Review:
A movie about chastity, sexual objectification, the internet, depersonalization, being terminally online, and disassociative personalities. What happens when the vicarious vessel we live through, the ideal of chastity, betrays that ideal by having its own will? Has the internet become a way for the most mentally afflicted to aggregate and multiply their effects? Or was it always like that?

Satoshi Kon has created perhaps the perfect psychological thriller. One that plays with the viewer's perception of reality and makes them question what is happening after the credits roll. It's a movie about control, reliving a glorious past vicariously, agency, sexuality, violence, and who we are.

The central question being asked here is: who are you? The refrain is repeated throughout the movie. Who are you, the viewer? Do your collection of continuous memories constitute an identity? Can you even trust those memories? Are dreams any less than the waking world? The dreams of our imagination or even the dreams of sleep?

Perfect Blue asks all of these questions.

Name: Frankenstein
Review:
Extremely underwhelming. Isaac's performance was too hammy. The monster's design was too clean. A lot of nitpicky plot points make no sense (outside of being faithful to the material). Unnecessary love triangle. Unnecessary love between Elizabeth and the monster.

Take Shelley's Frankenstein. Remove all of the philosophical depth. No questions about mortality, creation, suffering, existence. Make it just a revenge plot.

That's this.

The more I watch of Del Toro the more I realize that the man should have as few creative liberties with a script as possible. He is just not a good script writer. He's a fantastic director with a keen visual eye and a great style. But the moment he starts writing everything goes by the wayside.

I really hoped for more out of this one. It pales when compared to Egger's Nosferatu.

Name: No Other Choice
Review:
A social commentary on techno-feudalism wrapped in a black comedy crime thriller. Some of the most striking transitions & modern editing I've ever seen. Gorgeously shot. At once astoundingly hilarious & simultaneously horrifying.

At it's heart a critique of what it takes to win the zero sum game job market in the AI era. Are you truly willing to do what it takes to succeed in an era that sees the Technique of technology consuming all of the world's resources to deposit it as capital in the pocketbooks of the elite?

Never before has society had more immediately available luxuries and efficiencies. Yet, we live in a constant state of stress since we own nothing. We own nothing and are legally regulated out of directly accessing resources. So we are forced to participate in a dog-eat-dog system with fewer and fewer winners.

No Other Choice demonstrates the ethical choices winners must make. What does it take to actually succeed in modern capitalism?

Name: Resurrection
Review:
Seen at the National Museum of Asian Art, Freer Gallery:

The motion picture itself is a kind of rebellion against the ephemral nature of life. Everything that lives ultimately dies and is erased. A film is an attempt to capture a microcosm, to construct an ideal simulacrum of life and render it available for repeated future viewings.

This movie is a celebration of cinema's rebellion against transcience & a meditation on the beauty of impermanent things.

I don't typically enjoy anthologies. I would rather have one fully fleshed out idea than several half-baked ones. And each of the five stories here could have been their own movie.

What makes Resurrection unique is the clear central theme & persistent character of the delieriant. It is him dying & being reborn until the end of time, experiencing countless transient moments. Some of them are truly horrific, whereas others are full of indescribable joy.

Somehow Bi Gan has done the unthinkable. In a 2 1/2 hour runtime, he has crafted an amazing silent short, a supernatural crime noir, a meditative Buddhist ghost story, a charming adopted son crime drama, and a vampire romance. All within the context of a sci-fi dystopia. 

Typically, these kinds of films can come off as incredibly disjointed. That was my problem with Coogler's Sinners - too many good ideas packed into one story. Bi Gan could certainly have turned Resurrection into a series of films. Yet, there is a kind of emotional coherence & plot muddiness that makes this work.

Resurrection is also full of some of the best cinematography the medium has ever known. It is as if Bi Gan was able to distill some of the greatest shots in cinema history & give himself a canvas to weave them all together. Whether the shocking image of a Chinese detective in '60s clothing cutting open a covert operative only to catch aflame from the mystical dimension underneath his skin to a haunted Buddhist temple in the early morning being speckled by snow to the image of an estranged daughter's final burnt letter floating out of a box into the wind or a vampire crime overlord singing karaoke as his goons beat a man almost to death. Each of these pistáches is brought together in this kalodeiscopic tapestry of cinematic excellence.

In the end, Bi Gan pays his respects to the audience themselves. Casting us as beings of pure light in the cathedral of art, as each moviegoer fades into nothingness.

An absolutely singular ode to the always fading beauty of life & cinema.
